AASLD AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Primary Biliary Cholangitis
  • Source: Hepatology, 2026 (Vol. 00, Issue 00)
  • Topic: Diagnosis, treatment, risk stratification, symptom management, and post-transplantation care of adults with PBC
  • Author(s): Levy C, Mayo MJ, Carey EJ, Chen VL, Assis DN, Goel A, Sedki M, Sultan S, Taddei T, Bittermann T, Davitkov P
1. Disease Overview
  • Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) --> chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease
  • Characterized by progressive destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts --> fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver failure
  • Predominant demographic: women aged 40–70 years
  • Female-to-male ratio --> narrowing reported worldwide
  • Key symptoms: fatigue, pruritus (most debilitating)
  • Significant quality of life impairment independent of disease stage
  • Progressive fibrosis --> cirrhosis --> liver transplantation or death
1.1. Disease Burden
  • Up to 40% of PBC patients --> inadequate response to first-line therapy
  • Lower MELD scores relative to true disease burden --> higher waitlist mortality
  • Pruritus in refractory form --> itself an indication for liver transplantation
1.2. Key Clinical Challenges
  • Delayed diagnosis, especially in AMA-negative patients
  • Assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)
  • Risk stratification for disease progression
  • Treatment of inadequate responders
  • Management of cholestatic pruritus
  • Prevention of recurrent PBC after transplantation
2. Diagnosis of PBC
2.1. AMA-Positive Disease
  • Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) --> defining serologic marker for majority of PBC cases
  • Enables noninvasive diagnosis in most patients
2.2. AMA-Negative Disease (Rec. 1)
  • Requires additional diagnostic workup
  • PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies: anti-sp100 and anti-gp210
2.2.1. Diagnostic Accuracy
  • Anti-sp100: pooled sensitivity 22.7% (95% CI: 12.9–36.6%), pooled specificity 96.5% (95% CI: 93.9–98.0%)
  • Anti-gp210: pooled sensitivity 19.7% (95% CI: 10.2–34.6%), pooled specificity 99.0% (95% CI: 97.7–99.6%)
  • Sensitivity range across studies:
  • Anti-sp100: 2.6% to 64.7%
  • Anti-gp210: 0% to 60%
2.2.2. Absolute Effects at 1% Prevalence
  • Anti-sp100: ~227 true-positive and ~773 false-negative per 100,000 tested
  • Anti-gp210: ~197 true-positive and ~803 false-negative per 100,000 tested
  • Anti-sp100: ~3,465 false-positive per 100,000 tested
  • Anti-gp210: ~990 false-positive per 100,000 tested
2.2.3. Clinical Application
  • Tests best applied in evaluation of suspected cholestatic liver disease, not general population screening
  • High specificity (≥95%) --> positive result supports diagnosis without biopsy
  • Low sensitivity (~20%) --> negative results should not preclude further evaluation including liver biopsy
  • Positive result may obviate need for biopsy and allow earlier therapy initiation
2.3. Diagnostic Criteria Summary
  • Chronic ALP elevation > ULN, hepatic origin, without biliary obstruction evidence
  • No alternative explanation for cholestasis
3. First-Line Therapy: Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA) - Rec. 2
3.1. Recommendation
  • Strong recommendation for UDCA vs no treatment in treatment-naïve PBC
  • Certainty of evidence: moderate
  • First-line therapy for all patients --> should be offered at diagnosis
3.2. Dosing
  • 13–15 mg/kg/day --> standard dosing
  • Increasing dosage beyond 15 mg/kg/d --> not indicated
  • Continuation warranted even with persistent ALP elevation (sustained survival benefits)
3.3. Evidence Summary
  • 16 RCTs analyzed (1,447 participants)
  • Trial duration: 3–92 months (median 24 months)
  • Most trials conducted before contemporary second-line therapies
3.3.1. Biochemical Effects
  • Serum bilirubin: mean reduction 8.69 µmol/L (0.5 mg/dL)
  • Serum ALP: mean reduction 257 U/L
  • Histologic progression: 23.5% vs 38.2% (RR, 0.62; 95% CI: 0.44–0.88)
  • Absolute difference: 145 fewer individuals with histologic progression per 1,000 treated
3.3.2. Clinical Outcomes
  • All-cause mortality: 6.4% vs 6.6% (RR, 0.97; 95% CI: 0.67–1.42)
  • All-cause mortality or LT: 12.1% vs 12.6% (RR, 0.96; 95% CI: 0.74–1.25)
  • No improvement in pruritus (RR, 0.96; 95% CI: 0.84–1.09)
  • No improvement in fatigue (RR, 0.90; 95% CI: 0.81–1.00)
3.3.3. Safety Profile
  • SAEs: 13.5% vs 15.6% (RR, 0.87; 95% CI: 0.68–1.12)
  • Non-SAEs: 4.2% vs 2.8% (RR, 1.46; 95% CI: 0.83–2.56)
  • Non-SAEs include: diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, possible weight gain
  • Generally well tolerated
3.4. Long-Term Observational Data
  • Global PBC Study Group: 3,902 individuals
  • UDCA associated with lower risk of LT or death (HR, 0.46)
  • 5-year number needed to treat: 11 to prevent 1 LT or death
  • Benefit even higher among higher-risk individuals (cirrhosis, elevated ALP)
3.5. Key Principles
  • UDCA improves liver chemistries
  • Delays histologic progression
  • Improves transplantation-free survival
  • Even partial biochemical improvement --> better outcomes vs no therapy
  • Inadequate response should not prompt discontinuation --> consider adjunctive second-line therapy
4. Risk Stratification: Liver Stiffness Measurement (LSM) - Rec. 3
4.1. Recommendation
  • Conditional recommendation for LSM to improve prognostication in PBC
  • Certainty of evidence: moderate
4.2. Key Threshold
  • LSM ≥10 kPa by VCTE --> increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes
  • Patients with LSM ≥10 kPa may warrant closer monitoring and/or therapy escalation
4.3. Evidence Summary
  • 3 cohort studies with 3,698 participants
  • Pooled HR: 1.07 (95% CI: 1.05–1.08) per 1-kPa increase in LSM
  • Outcome: composite of decompensation, LT, or death
4.3.1. Published Cutoff Range
  • Studies used cutoffs from 9.3 to 11.0 kPa
  • Guideline suggests 10 kPa as reasonable consensus threshold
4.3.2. Serial LSM Considerations
  • Most recent LSM --> more strongly associated with outcomes than change between measures
  • Optimal frequency not well-defined
  • VCTE frequency should be based on:
  • Fibrosis severity
  • Probability of meaningful LSM change
4.4. Clinical Recommendations for Monitoring
  • Annual VCTE recommended in:
  • People with change in therapy
  • People with LSM ≥10 kPa
  • Case-by-case monitoring for LSM between 7–10 kPa
4.4.1. Treatment Response Data
  • Seladelpar study (post hoc analysis, 114 participants):
  • Baseline LSM <10.7 kPa: 15% (8/84) progressed to ≥10.7 kPa over 36 months
  • Baseline LSM ≥10.7 kPa: 43% (13/30) decreased to <10.7 kPa
  • Most change occurred by 12 months of treatment
4.4.2. Obeticholic Acid Study (Italian multicenter, 255 patients)
  • Mean starting LSM: 10 kPa
  • POISE responders: –0.48 kPa/y
  • POISE nonresponders: +0.33 kPa/y
4.5. Limitations
  • LSM may be less reliable with cholestasis (ALP ≥1.5× ULN or elevated bilirubin)
  • Accuracy affected by: body habitus, liver inflammation, nonfasting status, operator expertise
  • Availability and cost vary across settings
5. Second-Line Therapy: PPAR Agonists - Rec. 4
5.1. Recommendation
  • Conditional recommendation for PPAR agonists (elafibranor, seladelpar) in patients with:
  • Inadequate response to UDCA --> add-on therapy
  • Intolerance to UDCA --> monotherapy alternative
  • Certainty of evidence: low
5.2. Assessment of Response
  • Evaluate biochemical response at minimum 6 months, no later than 12 months after initiation
  • Inadequate response definition: failure to achieve:
  • Serum ALP < 1.5–1.67× ULN
  • Normal total bilirubin
  • At 12 months
5.3. Treatment Goals
  • Normalization of serum ALP --> ideal goal when possible
  • Particularly desirable for patients with LSM ≥10 kPa
5.4. FDA-Approved Agents
Agent Dosage Approval Status
Elafibranor 80 mg/day Accelerated FDA approval
Seladelpar 10 mg/day Accelerated FDA approval
5.5. Off-Label Options
  • Fenofibrate and bezafibrate (PPAR agonists) sometimes used off-label
  • Less extensively studied than newer agents
  • Bezafibrate not commercially available in US
5.6. Evidence: Phase 3 RCTs
5.6.1. Biochemical Response (Primary Endpoint)
  • Elafibranor: RR, 6.26 (95% CI: 2.39–16.39) --> 387 additional biochemical responders per 1,000 treated
  • Seladelpar: RR, 4.20 (95% CI: 2.11–8.36) --> 529 additional biochemical responders per 1,000 treated
5.6.2. ALP Normalization
  • Seladelpar: RR, 32.34 (95% CI: 4.52–231.64) --> 27 more per 1,000 treated
  • Elafibranor: RR, 9.32 (95% CI: 1.22–70.95) --> 12 more per 1,000 treated
5.6.3. Safety Profile
  • Seladelpar: no increase in SAEs (RR, 0.88; 95% CI: 0.32–2.44)
  • Elafibranor: no increase in SAEs (RR, 0.77; 95% CI: 0.32–1.88)
  • No increased treatment discontinuation
  • Lower incidences of drug-induced liver injury and muscle toxicity vs fibrates (indirect comparison)
5.7. Evidence: Bezafibrate
5.7.1. Biochemical Effects
  • ALP reduction from baseline: 49.5%
  • ALP normalization: 61.8% vs 15.6% with placebo
  • Pooled RR: 4.27 (95% CI: 2.37–7.66)
5.7.2. Safety
  • SAEs: 15.8% vs 15.9% (pooled OR, 1.16; 95% CI: 0.60–2.23)
  • Myalgia: 10.1% vs 5.4% (pooled OR, 2.17; 95% CI: 0.73–6.48)
  • Serum creatinine rise: ~3–5%
  • Rhabdomyolysis: rare (1/50 on concomitant statin therapy)
5.8. Evidence: Fenofibrate
  • ALP normalization RR: 2.13 (95% CI: 1.21–2.64) --> 165 more responders per 1,000 treated
  • Transaminase and creatinine elevations: predominantly low-grade and transient
  • Discontinuation for adverse events: rare (OR, 7.59; 95% CI: 0.47–121)
  • No rhabdomyolysis reported
5.9. Pruritus Effects
  • Seladelpar: statistically significant reduction in pruritus (WI-NRS)
  • Bezafibrate: superior to placebo for moderate-severe pruritus (21-day RCT)
  • Elafibranor: improvement in 5-D Itch Scale and PBC-40 itch domains
5.10. Monitoring on Second-Line Therapy
  • Quarterly laboratory testing during first year (expert opinion)
  • Less frequent monitoring once clinical benefits and tolerability established
  • Do not use in pregnancy, breastfeeding, decompensated cirrhosis (lack of safety data)
6. Pruritus Management: Linerixibat - Rec. 5
6.1. Recommendation
  • Conditional recommendation for linerixibat in moderate to severe cholestatic pruritus
  • Certainty of evidence: low
  • Patient values important: higher value on avoiding GI side effects or costs --> may reasonably choose not to use
6.2. Dosing
  • 40 mg twice daily
  • Trial duration: 2–12 weeks sufficient to assess efficacy and tolerability
  • Longer-term continuation based on clinical response
6.3. Evidence: Phase 2b and Phase 3 RCTs
  • 296 patients with PBC and WI-NRS score ≥4 (moderate to severe)
  • Assessed at 40 mg twice daily dosage
6.3.1. Efficacy Outcomes
  • WI-NRS reduction: 0.78 points (95% CI: –1.25 to –0.31) on 11-point scale
  • ≥2-point WI-NRS improvement: RR, 1.11 (95% CI: 0.93–1.32)
  • ≥3-point WI-NRS improvement: RR, 1.30 (95% CI: 1.00–1.69)
  • PBC-40 Itch score: no difference (MD, –0.66; 95% CI: –1.42 to 0.19)
  • Sleep interference improvement: 0.52 points (Sleep Disturbance NRS)
6.3.2. Safety/Harms
  • Diarrhea: RR, 3.57 (95% CI: 2.43–5.23)
  • Abdominal pain: RR, 3.67 (95% CI: 1.57–8.60)
  • Discontinuation due to adverse effects: RR, 2.92 (95% CI: 1.24–6.90)
  • Magnitude of harms deemed moderate by expert panel
6.4. Clinical Considerations
  • Strong placebo effect observed (especially in phase 3)
  • Improvement seen after 2 weeks, continued through ~12 weeks
  • Maximum diarrhea scores --> at week 3
  • 86% of patients in phase 3 study reported diarrhea resolution
6.4.1. Management Strategies
  • Temporary dose reduction if needed
  • Loperamide and/or dicyclomine for GI symptoms
  • Bile acid binding resins sometimes used
6.5. Limitations of Evidence
  • Insufficient evidence for mild cholestatic pruritus
  • No comparative studies to historical treatments (bile acid resins, rifampin)
  • Safety in decompensated cirrhosis unknown
  • Only FDA-approved treatment for PBC-related pruritus at time of publication
7. Post-Transplantation Care: UDCA Prophylaxis - Rec. 6
7.1. Recommendation
  • Conditional recommendation for UDCA prophylaxis to prevent recurrence and graft failure
  • Certainty of evidence: very low
  • Start as soon as possible after LT at 13–15 mg/kg/day
7.2. Evidence Summary
  • No RCTs identified
  • 2 comparative retrospective cohort studies (1,084 patients total)
  • Diagnosis of rPBC: clinical, serologic, and histopathologic findings
7.2.1. Global PBC Study Group (2020)
  • 790 patients transplanted for PBC, followed ≥1 year
  • 24% received UDCA prophylaxis (10–15 mg/kg/d) within 2 weeks after LT
  • Practice variation: 4/16 centers routinely started UDCA; 12 did not
7.2.2. Outcomes
  • rPBC: RR, 0.73 (95% CI: 0.54–1.00) in 2020 study alone
  • Graft failure: RR, 0.35 (95% CI: 0.15–0.79)
  • All-cause mortality: RR, 0.78 (95% CI: 0.40–1.52)
  • Liver-related mortality: RR, 1.10 (95% CI: 0.85–1.44)
7.2.3. Adjusted Outcomes (2020 Study)
  • rPBC: adjusted HR, 0.41
  • Graft loss: adjusted HR, 0.33
  • Liver-related death: adjusted HR, 0.69
  • Survival gain: 2.26 years over 20-year period
7.3. Safety Profile
  • No studies on harms in post-transplant setting specifically
  • Nontransplant data: no increase in SAEs (RR, 0.87; 95% CI: 0.68–1.12)
  • UDCA has extremely favorable safety profile
  • Minimal interactions with typical post-transplant medications
7.4. Natural History of rPBC
  • Median time to recurrence: 3–6 years
  • 10 years post-LT: ~20–30% develop rPBC
  • 20 years post-LT: ~50% develop rPBC
  • Diagnosis based on histology (lymphoid infiltrates, granulomatous/lymphocytic destructive cholangitis ± ductopenia)
  • AMAs not helpful after transplantation
7.4.1. Impact of rPBC
  • Progressive fibrosis leading to cirrhosis
  • Graft loss HR: 2.01
  • Decreased patient survival HR: 1.72
8. Clinical Decision Support Tool Summary
8.1. Diagnostic Algorithm
  • Suspected PBC --> check AMA
  • AMA positive --> initiate UDCA 13–15 mg/kg/day
  • AMA negative --> test for sp100 and gp210 antibodies
  • If positive --> confirmed PBC
  • If negative with strong clinical suspicion --> liver biopsy
8.2. Monitoring Schedule
  • Liver enzymes: every 3 months for first year
  • Assess response: at 6–12 months (earlier if high-risk features: LSM ≥10 kPa, age <62)
  • Ongoing risk stratification: annually or q1–3 years
8.3. Treatment Escalation Algorithm
  • Adequate response to UDCA --> continue management
  • Inadequate response or intolerance:
  • Add PPAR agonist (elafibranor 80 mg/day or seladelpar 10 mg/day)
  • Or monotherapy if UDCA-intolerant
  • Consider clinical trials or alternative PPAR agonist if inadequate response to first
8.4. Pruritus Management
  • Moderate-to-severe pruritus --> shared decision making for pharmacologic therapy
  • Start PPAR agonist if also inadequate response/intolerance to UDCA
  • Linerixibat 40 mg twice daily as option for cholestatic pruritus
9. Evidence Quality Assessment (GRADE)
9.1. Certainty Levels
Level Description
High Very confident true effect close to estimate
Moderate Moderately confident; true likely close to estimate
Low Limited confidence; true may be substantially different
Very Low Very little confidence; likely substantially different
9.2. Recommendation Strengths
Strength Implication
Strong ("we recommend") Most individuals should receive intervention; formal decision aids not likely needed
Conditional ("we suggest") Different choices appropriate for different patients; use shared decision making
9.3. Evidence Limitations in This Guideline
  • Most diagnostic studies: case-control designs (not prospective)
  • RCTs for UDCA: median duration ~2 years insufficient for long-term outcomes
  • PPAR agonist trials: surrogate biochemical endpoints vs patient-important outcomes
  • Small sample sizes and low event rates for safety outcomes
  • Open-label designs for some fibrate studies
10. Key Evidence Gaps and Future Research Needs
10.1. Diagnosis
  • Better prevalence estimates for AMA-negative PBC among cholestatic patients
  • Combined or sequential testing algorithms for anti-gp210 and anti-sp100
  • Downstream consequences of false-positive results
10.2. UDCA Therapy
  • Biomarkers predicting UDCA nonresponse before treatment initiation
  • Benefit in advanced decompensated cirrhosis (underrepresented)
10.3. LSM/Prognostication
  • Alternative modalities: shear wave elastography, MR elastography
  • Prognostic accuracy in context of newer PPAR agonist therapies
  • Stopping/continuation rules for pharmacotherapy based on LSM
10.4. Second-Line Therapy
  • Relationship between biochemical response and clinical outcomes (transplant-free survival)
  • Criteria for initiating therapy at ALP 1.0–1.5× ULN in high-risk groups
  • Role of PPAR agonists for pruritus despite adequate biochemical response
10.5. Pruritus Management
  • Comparative studies to historical treatments (bile acid resins, rifampin)
  • Safety/efficacy of combining IBAT inhibitors with newer PPAR agonists
  • Biomarkers predicting response to IBAT inhibitors
  • Optimal dosing strategies and intermittent vs continuous therapy
10.6. Post-Transplant Care
  • Which patients benefit most from prophylaxis (older age vs young)
  • Parameters for when to stop UDCA
  • Age threshold below which benefit becomes trivial
11. Key Statistical Thresholds and Cutoffs Used in Guideline
Parameter Threshold Clinical Significance
ALP response <1.5–1.67× ULN + normal bilirubin at 12 months Inadequate vs adequate response
LSM (VCTE) ≥10 kPa High-risk for unfavorable outcomes
WI-NRS (pruritus) ≥4 out of 10 Moderate-to-severe pruritus
WI-NRS improvement ≥2–4 points Clinically meaningful
Treatment response 6 months minimum, 12 months maximum Assessment timing
12. Key References to Studies
  • Global PBC Study Group: 3,902 patients (long-term UDCA outcomes)
  • Cochrane review: 16 RCTs, 1,447 participants (UDCA efficacy)
  • ENHANCE/ELATIVE/RESPONSE trials: Phase 3 PPAR agonist studies
  • GLIMMER/GLISTEN trials: Linerixibat phase 2b and phase 3 studies
  • BEZURSO trial: Bezafibrate in inadequate responders

FIGURE 1: Clinical decision support tool. (1) Chronic ALP elevation greater than the ULN, of hepatic origin, without evidence of biliary obstruction, and without alternative explanation. (2) Assess response at 6 months if high-risk features are present, including but not limited to LSM ≥ 10 kPa and age < 62 years. (3) Itching severity is determined by the person living with PBC. Shared decision making is used to determine need for pharmacologic therapy and choice among available options. The guideline panel suggests starting with addition of a PPAR agonist if the individual also has inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA. The role of a PPAR agonist to manage pruritus in the setting of an adequate response to UDCA is not yet defined. (4) Inadequate response: failure to achieve serum ALP levels < 1.5–1.67 times the ULN and normal total bilirubin levels at 12 months. (5) Clinicians may choose alternative forms to manage pruritus based on the tradeoff between side effects and persistence of itching. NOTE. GRADE Strength of recommendation (strong vs conditional) is shown in each box and certainty of evidence is indicated by the cross-filled circles. For definitions see Table 3.
